ann_89.text: Calls to customer service clearly add to the predicted chance from about 3 calls upwards: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical customer from about 1% to about 14%.

Daytime minutes clearly add to it only once they rise above about 198, in an uneven way across customers (from 0 to 271 minutes, about 1% to 9%), and more so if evening minutes are above 201 (about 1% to 7%, against 1% to 2%).

Smaller effects through this part, each changing the predicted chance only slightly for a typical customer: more daytime, evening and night-time minutes raise it in an uneven way; going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls raises it slowly at first, then faster; and a voice-mail plan lowers it.

This part acts on 1795 of 4000 customers (453 of them left), and for a typical one (in New Jersey, with two customer-service calls and about 206 daytime minutes) it raises the predicted chance only slightly, from about 2% to about 3%.

For customers without a voice-mail plan, a daytime charge above about $40.05 (between $37.18 and $55.40 for different customers) raises it only slightly, in an uneven way, and being in Louisiana or South Dakota lowers it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_90.text: This part acts on 380 of 4000 customers, and 161 of them left.
For a typical customer it acts on (in Illinois, with an international plan), it clearly raises the predicted chance from about 1% to about 24%.
An international plan clearly raises it from about 1% to about 15% for a typical customer, and even more so for customers in Iowa (about 1% to 31%).
For the customer it acts on, being in Iowa raises it from about 24% to about 38%, and being in Missouri raises it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_91.text: This part acts on 3988 of 4000 customers (566 of them left), and for a typical one it lowers the predicted chance only slightly, from about 2% to about 1% (on the training data only).
Through it, a higher daytime charge lowers the predicted chance only slightly, from about $15.06 upwards, slowly at first, then faster (on the training data only).
More night-time minutes also lower it slightly, in stages, from about 130 minutes upwards (on the training data only).
International minutes add nothing until about 12 minutes, then raise it slightly and steadily (on the training data only).
The evening charge adds nothing until about $19.04, then lowers it slightly and steadily (on the training data only).
Being in Pennsylvania, Tennessee or Indiana raises it only slightly, and in Indiana night-time minutes matter slightly more, in an uneven way (on the training data only).

ann_92.text: Through this part, being in Washington raises the predicted chance for a typical customer only slightly, from about 1% to about 5%, and Louisiana, New Jersey, South Dakota, Kentucky, Colorado, Ohio and Vermont change it only slightly (on the training data only).
More evening calls barely change it: they lower it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_93.text: Area code 510 lowers the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only).
One small part barely changes the predictions.

ann_94.text: A longer account raises the predicted chance only slightly, with nothing until an account length of about 60, then steadily (on the training data only).
This part acts on 3341 of 4000 customers, and 484 of them left.

ann_95.text: In this straight-line part, voice-mail messages and plan, international charge, calls and minutes, evening and night-time minutes, account length and the state each change the predicted chance only slightly, the numeric ones steadily (on the training data only).

ann_96.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the predicted chance for a typical customer from about 1% to about 15%.
Going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls raises it slightly, slowly at first, then faster (about 1% to 3%).
More daytime minutes raise it slightly, in an uneven way (about 1% to 3%), and a voice-mail plan lowers it slightly.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only): more voice-mail messages and a higher international charge raise it steadily; each extra international call lowers it by about the same amount; more international minutes raise it slowly at first, then faster; a longer account raises it in stages; a higher evening charge adds nothing until about $19.04, then lowers it steadily; and more evening calls barely change it.
Being in Washington raises it slightly, to about 5% for a typical customer, and the other states and area code 510 also change it only slightly (on the training data only).
It ignores the number of daytime and night-time calls and total night-time charge.

ann_89.original:
Nonlinear usage core and the only source of the network's gain over a linear model. 879 = relu(-1.085 + 0.621 dayMin + 0.254 nightMin - 0.968 voiceMailPlan + 0.547*7558 - 0.075 state18 - 0.12 relu(state18 - 0.36)), with 7558 = relu(0.519 + 0.781 eveMin + 1.254*1406) and 1406 = relu(-0.531 + 0.592 dayCharge - 0.856 state41), a second day hinge above dayCharge z ~ 0.9 (dayCharge = dayMinutes after z-scoring). Readouts: +2.305*879, a service-calls gate +3.524*relu(-0.378 + 0.646 CSC - 3.643*879) that only opens when 879 is ~0, and a convex second hinge +3.622*relu(-0.895 + 1.415 relu(-0.399 + 1.258*879)) for the heaviest users. So: P(churn) rises steeply with total (mostly day) usage for customers WITHOUT a voicemail plan, and, for customers below the usage hinge, with customer-service calls from 3-4 calls up.

Evidence (train, n=4000): Train n=4000. 879 is active for 41.4% of no-voicemail rows and 0.6% of voicemail-plan rows. Mean usageResponse logit by day-minutes decile (no voicemail plan): 0.43, 0.62, 0.48, 0.59, 0.48, 0.72, 0.84, 1.10, 1.89, 6.61; voicemail plan: 0.27-0.71 flat. Observed churn by decile: no-vm 0.11, 0.19, 0.08, 0.12, 0.08, 0.07, 0.06, 0.09, 0.22, 0.61; vm 0.04-0.11 flat -- the vm x heavy-day-usage interaction is in the data. In the top decile 10552 is on (mean 0.995) and supplies most of the +6.6. CSC gate: with 879 off, the gate adds 0, 0, 0, +1.16, +2.91, +4.65, +6.39 logit at 0..6 calls; observed churn 0.058, 0.047, 0.052, 0.047, 0.536, 0.632, 0.773, so the threshold is between 3 and 4 calls and the +1.16 at 3 calls is not supported by the data (churn 0.047 at 3 calls). With 879 on, the gate is mostly shut. Sensitivity (get_viz_summary, train): 879 most sensitive to voiceMailPlan 0.29, dayMinutes 0.19, eveMinutes 0.12; 4344 to CSC 0.10. Local AUC (train): full 0.926; this child replaced by its least-squares linear fit 0.831; mean-ablated 0.594; restored alone onto the all-linear model +0.094 (the whole nonlinear gain 0.095). Linear R2 0.37. Parts restored alone: direct 879 +0.053, CSC gate +0.040, second hinge +0.071 (overlapping). state18 and state41 enter here: state41 shuts the 1406 day hinge (on 2 saturated heavy users, logit -3.1/-5.5 but p 0.998-1.0, negligible); state18 lowers 879 and gives two non-churning customers p 0.43->0.11 and 0.56->0.016.

ann_96.original:
Root: P(churn) = sigmoid(-2.009 + usageResponse + intlPlanSwitch + usageHinges + stateUnits + areaCodeUnits + accountLengthUnits + linearBackbone). Purely additive in the logit: the seven children share no hidden nodes and interact only through the output sigmoid. All nonlinearity that matters is inside usageResponse (voicemail-gated usage hinge, convex top-usage hinge, and a service-calls gate that opens from 3-4 calls only below the usage hinge). The intl plan is a flat +3.0 offset; the other children are near-affine corrections and per-state offsets. 27 unconnected inputs (22 states, areaCode415, totalDayCalls, totalNightCalls, totalNightCharge) are zero-effect entries.

Evidence: Train n=4000: AUC 0.926 (refit L2 logistic regression 0.843). Every top-level child replaced by its least-squares linear fit jointly: 0.831. summary.text: For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, with no international or voice-mail plan, one call to customer service and median usage, such as about 180 daytime minutes), having an international plan clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 1% to about 15%.
Calls to customer service clearly add to it from about 3 calls upwards: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical customer from about 1% to about 14%.

Daytime minutes clearly add to it only once they rise above about 198, in an uneven way across customers (from 0 to 271 minutes, about 1% to 9%), and the rise is clearly larger if evening minutes are above 201 (about 1% to 7%, against 1% to 2%).
The rise for an international plan is clearly larger for customers in Iowa (about 1% to 31%).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only): being in Washington rather than West Virginia raises it to about 5%; more voice-mail messages raise it steadily; a longer account raises it in stages; and more evening calls barely change it.
The model ignores the number of daytime and night-time calls and total night-time charge.

parts.original_hypothesis:
